text.tspan: Fifty-plus executive dashboards for U.S. hospital
systems. The team needed one answer to "is this
chart readable?" I led the study that produced it,
then built the Figma system that made it the default.
Client data can't be shown publicly. This page is the
— the rules, the reasoning, and charts rebuilt from synthetic data that obey them. Real
Executives read these charts to make decisions with real
consequences — often through a boardroom projector's washed-out
colour, sometimes printed to greyscale, occasionally on a phone.
Accessibility was handled per-dashboard, by whoever designed it.
Everyone made reasonable choices. Collectively there was no standard
— and no definition of what "compliant" even meant for a
is written for text and UI components, not for eleven categorical series
WCAG tells you a label needs 4.5:1. It doesn't tell you
how many series a colourblind reader can tell apart.
I audited the dashboards already shipping, not a hypothetical. Three

Where the ceiling of five comes from
I'd been repeating "six" out of habit, so I checked. I solved for the best
achievable palette at each size and measured the worst pair under
MINIMUM PAIRWISE ΔE2000 ACROSS NORMAL, PROTAN, DEUTAN, TRITAN AND GREYSCALE
Six series cannot clear ΔE 10 in every mode — not with a
better palette, not with more care. Greyscale is the
binding constraint: six colours means six distinguishable

text.tspan: A standard nobody follows is a document. This one stuck because it
went into the Figma library the team already used: verified palettes as
styles, chart components with tints pre-applied, annotation patterns for
Designers stopped picking colours per chart. They picked a
component and compliance came with it.
Legacy dashboards didn't retro-fit themselves. And the ΔE 10 series
floor is my threshold, not a standards body's — I'd defend it, but it's a
judgement call and I flag it as one.
Checking the rules by hand was still slow. That led to the next project.
The tool I built to automate this audit — and the
